body.heading: Riding each other's air
paragraphs: As a bird flaps, its wingtips stir the air into swirling trails. Just behind and to the side of those wingtips, the swirls push air upward. A bird that positions itself in that rising air gets a little free lift with every flap, like a cyclist tucked into the slipstream of the rider ahead.

Studies of migrating ibises showed that birds time their flapping to catch these updrafts, and that the birds in a flock take turns at the front, where the work is hardest. The V is a shared arrangement: everyone saves energy, and the lead is passed around.

body.heading: Keeping in touch
paragraphs: The formation has a second benefit. From a V, each bird can see its neighbours and keep visual contact with the whole flock, which helps the group stay together and change direction smoothly.
The savings matter on journeys of thousands of kilometres. A flock flying in formation can travel considerably farther on the same stored energy than the same birds flying alone.

takeaway: Birds fly in a V to borrow lift from each other's wingtips, share the hardest work, and stay in sight of the flock.
